hook.text: A model's last layer gives every token in its vocabulary a score, called a logit. Something still has to pick one.

logits.text: Say the sentence so far is, her new pet is a. Cat scores three point two... and rock scores minus zero point four.

softmax.text: Softmax turns scores into probabilities. It raises e to each score, then divides by the total.

share.text: Cat gets sixty-five percent, three times dog's share from a gap of one point one. Rock gets under two.

picker.text: And the picking isn't done by the model. It's a few lines of code with a couple of settings... and it's why one prompt can give different answers.

divide.text: Temperature divides every score before the softmax. The order never changes... only the shape does.

low.text: Below one, the gaps grow. At zero point two, cat takes over ninety-nine percent.

greedy.text: At zero, it takes the top token every time. That's greedy decoding.

high.text: Above one, the gaps shrink. At one point five, rock climbs to almost five percent.

topp.text: Top p trims the tail before the draw. Keep the likeliest tokens until they cover ninety percent, and drop the rest.

topp-cut.text: At one point five, that keeps cat, dog and bird. Rock can't be drawn at all.

adapt.text: And the cut adapts. When the model's sure, one token covers ninety percent on its own. When it's torn between six, all six stay in.

runs.text: Still, every pick is a draw. Five runs over the same three close scores give five different strings.

compound.text: In a real model, each pick becomes context for the next, so two answers can agree for a sentence and then split completely.

hall-in.text: And the sampler always picks something, even when nothing true is on the list.

plausible.text: That explains hallucination. The model writes plausible continuations, and a plausible continuation of a question is an answer.

check.text: Whether a real answer exists isn't something it can check.

paris.text: The capital of France is... Paris. It's seen that millions of times.

chen.text: A twenty nineteen study on this by... Chen et al. found a twenty-three percent improvement. Just as fluent, and that study was never in its data.

shape.text: It's read millions of citations, so it nails the shape: names, a year, a journal. But nothing marks a fact as, I actually know this one.

risk.text: The risk isn't spread evenly, though. It climbs when the fact is rare, specific, or made of several parts, when it's past the training cutoff... and when the question assumes there's an answer.

score.text: The capital of France scores zero out of five. The name of the study that proved this? Four.

hedge.text: [curious] So why not just say, tell me if you don't know?

hedge-why.text: You'll get more hedges... but they don't land on the wrong answers, because nothing inside knows which ones are wrong.

works.text: What works is changing the task. Paste in the source. Ask for something you can check. Constrain the shape. And give it an exit, like, reply not found.

exit.text: It's picking a continuation either way, so hand it an easy, honest one.

ctx-in.text: Pasting in the source means filling the context window. And the window has limits of its own.

window.text: The context window is everything the model reads in one request: the system prompt, the documents, the history, the question... and the answer it writes, all from one budget.

fill.text: In a two hundred thousand token window, one long document leaves just six thousand three hundred tokens to answer in.

edge.text: And past the edge, nothing fades. It's simply not there. Apps quietly trim old turns to fit, which is how a long chat forgets its own beginning.

costs.text: Filling it isn't free, either. You pay for every input token, every turn. A five hundred thousand token document, over ten turns, is five million tokens billed, unless a cache steps in.

middle.text: And the model doesn't read it all equally well. Facts at the start and the end come back reliably. The middle sags. It's called lost in the middle.

permission.text: So a bigger window is permission, not a recommendation.

square.text: Why did long context take years to build? Every token attends to every other token, so the work grows with the square of the length.

square-num.text: From eight thousand tokens to a million is a hundred and twenty-five times the text... and over fifteen thousand times the work.

reason-in.text: Reasoning models spend tokens on purpose.

think.text: A reasoning model writes out its working before it answers: attempts, checks, corrections. Those are thinking tokens.

same.text: It's the same next-token machine, with nothing new inside. What changed is the training.

rl.text: It's rewarded for answers that can be checked, like math with a known result, or code that passes its tests. So habits like checking its own work get reinforced.

slip.text: Here it tries simple interest, catches the slip, and redoes it as compound growth.

returns.text: More thinking helps, up to a point. The first five hundred tokens buy nearly two thirds of the gain.

flat.text: Past eight thousand, doubling the budget buys nothing at all.

where.text: It pays off where steps can be checked, like math, code and planning. But no amount of thinking recalls a fact it never had.

overthink.text: And on an easy problem, more thinking can even talk it out of a right first answer.

bill.text: And thinking tokens are output tokens, billed whether you see them or not. In that answer, you'd read thirteen tokens and pay output prices for a hundred and nineteen.

effort.text: So set the lowest effort that passes your own tests, on purpose.

next.text: Every token the model reads, writes or thinks ends up on the bill. So what does a token actually cost?
